question.title: Pipeline as Code
question.scenario: Your team wants pipeline definitions version-controlled alongside application code, with reusable templates across multiple projects.
question.question-text: How should you implement pipeline as code?

choices.choice: Classic UI-based pipelines only
YAML pipelines with templates in a shared repository
PowerShell scripts without pipeline definitions
Manual build steps documented in wiki

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which pipeline format lives alongside your code in source control and supports shared definitions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: YAML pipelines store pipeline definitions as code in the repository, enabling version control, code review, and history. Templates in a shared repository provide reusable components (stages, jobs, steps) that multiple projects can reference, ensuring consistency.

ul.li: Template types: step, job, stage, and variable templates.
Extends templates enforce organizational standards on all pipelines.
Template parameters enable customization while maintaining structure.
Store templates in a dedicated repo with versioned releases.

question.title: Database DevOps
question.scenario: Your application uses Azure SQL Database. You need to automate schema changes, ensure backward compatibility during deployments, and enable rollback of database changes.
question.question-text: How should you implement database DevOps?

choices.choice: State-based approach with SSDT and incremental deployments
Manual SQL scripts run by DBAs
Direct production database modifications
Full database replacement with each deployment

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider a state-based approach where you define the desired schema and let tooling generate the diff scripts.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SQL Server Data Tools (SSDT) uses a state-based approach: define desired schema state, generate incremental migration scripts. Include database project in CI/CD pipeline. Use pre/post deployment scripts for data migrations. Design changes for backward compatibility (expand-contract pattern).

ul.li: State-based (SSDT): define target state, auto-generate diff scripts.
Migration-based (EF Migrations, Flyway): explicit up/down migration scripts.
Expand-contract: add new column, migrate data, remove old column in separate releases.
Always test migrations against production-like data volumes.

question.title: Application Performance Monitoring
question.scenario: Your web application needs end-to-end monitoring: request tracing, dependency tracking, exception logging, and performance metrics with alerting.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides comprehensive APM capabilities?

choices.choice: Windows Event Logs
Application Insights with distributed tracing
Custom logging to blob storage
Azure Monitor metrics only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which Azure service offers end-to-end request tracing, dependency mapping, and anomaly detection out of the box?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Application Insights is Azure's APM solution. It automatically tracks requests, dependencies (SQL, HTTP calls), exceptions, and custom metrics. Distributed tracing follows requests across services. Smart detection alerts on anomalies. Live metrics show real-time performance.

ul.li: Auto-instrumentation available for .NET, Java, Node.js, Python.
OpenTelemetry is becoming the standard; App Insights supports OTLP.
Application Map visualizes service dependencies and health.
Workspace-based App Insights uses Log Analytics for unified querying.

question.title: Test Automation Strategy
question.scenario: Your pipeline needs multiple test types: unit tests for fast feedback, integration tests for component interaction, and UI tests for end-to-end validation.
question.question-text: How should you organize tests in the pipeline?

choices.choice: Manual testing only
Only UI tests for complete coverage
Skip tests to speed up deployment
Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, minimal UI tests

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The test pyramid optimizes for fast feedback with unit tests and reduces slow, brittle UI tests.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The test pyramid recommends: many fast unit tests (base), moderate integration tests (middle), few slow UI/E2E tests (top). Unit tests run in CI for fast feedback. Integration tests validate component interactions. UI tests verify critical user journeys. This balances coverage with speed.

ul.li: Unit tests: isolated, fast, run on every commit.
Integration tests: test contracts between services, can use test containers.
E2E tests: slow, brittle; reserve for critical paths.
Parallelize test execution to reduce pipeline duration.

question.title: Deployment Rings
question.scenario: Your application serves millions of users globally. You want to minimize blast radius by deploying to progressively larger user groups, validating health at each stage.
question.question-text: What deployment pattern should you implement?

choices.choice: Ring-based deployment with progressive exposure
Simultaneous deployment to all users
Geographic deployment without validation
A/B testing without deployment stages

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about concentric circles of exposure, starting with the smallest audience and expanding outward.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Ring-based deployment defines concentric deployment stages: Ring 0 (internal/dogfood), Ring 1 (canary users), Ring 2 (early adopters), Ring 3 (all users). Each ring validates stability before expanding. This limits blast radius and enables early detection of issues before they affect all users.

ul.li: Microsoft uses rings internally for Windows and Azure deployments.
Ring criteria: internal employees, beta users, percentage rollout.
Bake time: wait period at each ring to observe metrics.
Feature flags can implement logical rings without infrastructure changes.

question.title: Inner Source
question.scenario: Your organization has multiple teams that could benefit from sharing and contributing to internal projects. You want to enable cross-team collaboration while maintaining code ownership.

choices.choice: Copy code between repositories
Strict team silos with no code sharing
All code in a single team's ownership
Inner source with discoverable repositories and contribution guidelines

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What if you applied open-source collaboration norms — discoverability, contribution guidelines, PRs — inside the company?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Inner source adopts open-source collaboration practices internally. Make repositories discoverable, document contribution guidelines (CONTRIBUTING.md), accept pull requests from other teams, and maintain clear ownership (CODEOWNERS). This enables reuse and collective improvement while preserving accountability.

ul.li: CODEOWNERS file defines required reviewers for specific paths.
README, CONTRIBUTING, and LICENSE files set expectations.
Trusted committers are non-owners with merge permissions.
GitHub/GitLab enterprise features support inner source patterns.

question.title: Infrastructure Deployment Pipeline
question.scenario: Your IaC code needs the same rigor as application code: validation, testing, approval for production, and change tracking.
question.question-text: How should you deploy infrastructure changes?

choices.choice: PR-based workflow with validation, what-if preview, and staged deployment
Direct deployment from developer machines
Azure Portal changes with manual documentation
Single branch with immediate production deployment

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about applying the same rigor to infrastructure changes as to application code: review, preview, then deploy.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Treat infrastructure code like application code. PRs trigger validation (syntax, linting). What-if/plan shows proposed changes without applying. Deploy to lower environments first, then production with approval. This provides change review, safe deployment, and audit trail.

ul.li: Bicep/ARM what-if: preview changes without deployment.
Terraform plan: show proposed changes; apply requires approval.
Policy compliance check as pipeline gate before deployment.
Drift detection: compare deployed state to code regularly.

question.title: Code Review Best Practices
question.scenario: Code reviews are becoming bottlenecks with long review times and inconsistent feedback. You need to improve review efficiency and quality.

choices.choice: Skip reviews for urgent changes
Large PRs reviewed by many people
Small PRs, automated checks, review guidelines, and CODEOWNERS
Only senior developers review code

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Small PRs are faster to review; automation catches style issues; guidelines ensure consistency.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Keep PRs small and focused (< 400 lines). Automate style/lint checks so reviewers focus on logic. Document review guidelines (what to look for, response time expectations). CODEOWNERS automatically assigns appropriate reviewers. Use PR templates to ensure context is provided.

ul.li: Research shows review quality drops significantly after 400 lines.
Stacked PRs: chain of dependent PRs for large changes.
Review time SLO: set expectations (e.g., first response within 24 hours).
Use suggestion feature for minor changes instead of comments.

question.title: Incident Management
question.scenario: When production incidents occur, your team needs clear escalation paths, communication channels, and post-incident learning processes.

choices.choice: Ignore incidents until customers complain
On-call rotation, incident response runbooks, and blameless postmortems
Management handles all incidents
Ad-hoc response by whoever is available

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Structured incident management includes defined roles, runbooks, and learning from incidents.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Establish on-call rotation with clear escalation paths. Create runbooks documenting common incident responses. During incidents, use defined roles (incident commander, communications). After resolution, conduct blameless postmortems focusing on systemic improvements, not individual blame.

ul.li: PagerDuty, OpsGenie integrate with Azure Monitor for alerting.
Incident severity levels define response urgency and communication.
Postmortem template: timeline, impact, root cause, action items.
Track action items to completion; incidents repeat without fixes.
